hints: Think about what must happen first inside the nucleus before any new protein like EPO can be made in larger amounts.
Link the EPO gene being switched on to making a messenger molecule needed for translation at the ribosome.
walkthrough:
Connect Low Oxygen To The Gene**
Low oxygen acts as a signal to increase production of EPO protein. Since a gene codes for a protein, the cell must increase expression of the EPO gene.

From Transcription To More mRNA**
Increased gene expression means more transcription of the EPO gene to make mRNA. That mRNA then passes to ribosomes for translation, so more EPO protein can be synthesised.
Final answer: The EPO gene is switched on / transcribed at a higher rate. More mRNA for EPO is made for translation into EPO protein.

hints: Picture where the vesicles start in the cytoplasm and where they need to end up to release their contents outside.
Recall the name of the process where a vesicle membrane becomes part of the cell surface membrane to release a protein.
walkthrough:
Move Vesicles To The Surface**
EPO is a large protein so it is packaged in secretory vesicles. These vesicles are moved through the cytoplasm to the plasma membrane.

Fuse And Release By Exocytosis**
The vesicle membrane fuses with the cell surface membrane. This opens the vesicle to the outside so EPO is released by exocytosis, a process requiring ATP.
Final answer: Vesicles move to the cell surface / plasma membrane and fuse with it, releasing EPO by exocytosis.

hints: Even though EPO reaches every cell in blood, think about what must be present on the surface for a cell to detect it.
Think about shape matching between a signalling molecule and its binding site, like a key fitting only one lock.
Consider which cells possess that matching site and what happens inside the cell after binding.
walkthrough:
Binding Needs A Complementary Receptor**
EPO acts at the cell surface by binding to receptors. Receptors have a specific shape complementary to EPO, so EPO fits into them.

Only Target Cells Have The Right Receptor**
Only particular target cells such as bone marrow cells have EPO-specific receptors. Other cells lack them, so EPO cannot bind to them.

Binding Triggers A Response Inside**
When EPO binds its receptor on a target cell, this is cell signalling that leads to specific responses inside that cell, such as stimulation to produce red blood cells.
Final answer: EPO binds to specific complementary receptors found only on target / bone marrow cells. Binding triggers cell signalling leading to responses within target cells only.

hints: Recall from the stem that EPO is described as a large glycoprotein and think about the structure of the phospholipid bilayer.
walkthrough:
Why A Large Protein Is Kept Out**
The cell surface membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with a hydrophobic core. EPO is a large hydrophilic glycoprotein, so it is too large and too water-soluble to diffuse through, and there is no transport protein for it. That is why it must act at the surface receptor instead.
Final answer: EPO is too large to pass through the membrane / is hydrophilic and cannot cross the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.

hints: Think of the general name for an undifferentiated cell that can divide by mitosis continuously and differentiate into specialised cells.
walkthrough:
Name The Undifferentiated Dividing Cell**
A cell that is undifferentiated, capable of continuous mitotic division and able to differentiate into red blood cells is a stem cell. In bone marrow these are haematopoietic stem cells.
Final answer: Stem cell / haematopoietic stem cell.

hints: Start by reading the y-values at weeks 0, 2, 4 and 6 before any EPO effect builds up, and note when the first injection arrow occurs.
Track the peak and the fall - find the highest mean Hb value and week, then the final value at week 10.
Link rising Hb to what EPO does to bone marrow cells and the Hb they contain.
Think about why Hb keeps rising for a week after the last injection and then falls when stimulation stops and old cells die.
walkthrough:
Describe The Baseline**
From week 0 to week 2 mean Hb concentration remains constant at about $12.6 \text{ g per kg body mass}$. This is before EPO injections start at week 2, when oxygen supply is sufficient so no extra EPO is needed.

Describe The Rise With Data**
After week 2 Hb rises steadily for 5 weeks to a peak of about $15.3 \text{ g per kg}$ at week 7, an increase of about $2.7 \text{ g per kg}$. It even keeps rising for one week after the final injection at week 6. Quote values to support the trend.

Explain The Rise**
Injected EPO binds target bone marrow cells and stimulates production of more red blood cells which contain haemoglobin. There is a time delay because mitosis, differentiation and haemoglobin production take time, so Hb builds up gradually and continues briefly after injections stop as immature cells mature.

Explain The Fall**
From week 7 to week 10 Hb falls to about $13.7 \text{ g per kg}$, a decrease of about $1.6 \text{ g per kg}$. Once injections stop, cell signalling stops and EPO is degraded, so no new stimulation occurs, while older short-lived red blood cells die and are not replaced at the same rate.

Final answer: Description: Hb constant at $12.6 \text{ g per kg}$ weeks 0-2, then rises to $15.3 \text{ g per kg}$ at week 7, then falls to $13.7 \text{ g per kg}$ at week 10. Explanation: EPO stimulates red blood cell production containing Hb; after injections stop signalling stops and short-lived red cells die, with a time delay for maturation.

hints: Compare air at sea level and at high altitude in terms of oxygen partial pressure and how much oxygen is available to breathe in.
Think about what lower available oxygen means for haemoglobin loading in the lungs.
Consider how making more of the oxygen-carrying pigment would compensate for that problem over time.
walkthrough:
Less Oxygen Available**
At high altitude the partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere is lower, so less oxygen is present in inhaled air and less oxygen is transported to tissues.

Haemoglobin Less Saturated**
With less oxygen available, haemoglobin has lower oxygen saturation in the lungs, so each red blood cell carries less oxygen.

More Carriers Compensate**
Increased EPO stimulates production of more red blood cells containing more haemoglobin. This compensation increases total oxygen-carrying capacity, helping maintain oxygen delivery despite low partial pressure.

Final answer: At altitude low partial pressure of oxygen means less oxygen inhaled and lower saturation of haemoglobin. More EPO produces more red blood cells containing haemoglobin to compensate and maintain oxygen delivery to tissues.
